name: Generalization
kick: large language models · first principles · learning the rules, not the strings
title: Generalization — why a model that learned something new handles things it never saw
lede: A model could ace every sentence in its training data by pure memorization and still fail on anything new. Generalization is the opposite: a model that truly learned language grasps the underlying rules well enough to handle new sentences it never saw before. Here is the problem it solves, why a single experiment proves it matters, where it breaks down, and why understanding this gap between memorization and learning drives almost everything in modern machine learning.
arc: Why the gap is the whole game

sections.h2: 1 · The problem — memorizing strings is not enough

blocks.html: A model could theoretically memorize every sentence it saw during training and produce them back perfectly. But what if it sees a novel sentence, one that was never in the training data? If all it did was memorize, it would be lost. And here lies the hard question: how can you tell whether a model has actually learned the underlying rules of language, or whether it has just memorized a bunch of strings? A model that memorizes cannot generalize; a model that generalizes has understood the pattern.

sections.h2: 2 · The reframe — test it on things it never saw

blocks.html: The experiment is simple in principle: take a model trained on a large dataset, and give it two kinds of new input it has never seen before. First, a sentence that is grammatically correct and uses real words, but is a novel combination — something the rules of language make sensible, even though this exact sentence did not appear in training. Second, a string that is just random noise: tokens jumbled with no grammar, no meaning, just chaos. If the model has learned the rules, the grammatical sentence should feel easy (the rules apply, so it should make sense), and the random noise should feel hard (no rules to lean on, so it should be lost). Mathematically, we measure this as 'loss' — how surprised the model is by each token. Lower loss means the model finds it expected; higher loss means it is shocked. The model that learned real rules will show a big gap between the loss on grammatical text and the loss on noise.

sections.h2: 3 · Seen on a real run — learned rules beat memorized strings

blocks.html: We ran the actual GPT-2, a language model with 124 million learned numbers, on two kinds of sentences it had never seen. One was a novel but grammatically correct sentence. The other was a string of random tokens. We measured how surprised the model was (loss) by each.

blocks.caption: Loss on a novel grammatical sentence vs. random tokens. Lower loss means less surprised. Numbers are the run's output.

blocks.html: The discovered fact: on a novel grammatical sentence, the loss is 6.24; on random tokens, the loss jumps to 13.71. That is more than twice as high. The gap is enormous. If GPT-2 had merely memorized training strings and not learned anything, it would be equally lost on both. Instead, the novel sentence — which follows the rules of language — feels almost natural to it, while random noise is bewildering.

sections.h2: 4 · Why the gap is the whole game

blocks.html: The gap proves generalization. The novel sentence obeys the rules the model learned during training — grammar, word order, syntax, the patterns that repeat across millions of examples. Because the model captured those rules, a new sentence built from them feels reasonable, even though it is a new combination. Random tokens have no rules; they are pure noise. The model cannot apply what it learned because there is nothing to apply; every token is a surprise. The larger the gap between learned-rule loss and noise loss, the more the model generalized rather than memorized. A model that memorized would treat them the same. A model that learned treats rules as easy and chaos as hard.

sections.h2: 5 · The one real weakness — generalization is bounded, and the line is blurry

blocks.html: Generalization has real limits. Models still fail on inputs far outside their training distribution — highly technical jargon they never saw, other languages, or adversarial inputs designed to break them. And the boundary between generalization and memorization is not clean. A model can memorize rare specifics (a particular person's biography) while also generalizing (grammar, syntax). The phenomenon of 'grokking' — where a model suddenly jumps from memorizing to generalizing after many steps of training — shows that the line between the two is context-dependent and can shift. Generalization is real and measurable, but it is not all-or-nothing; models live on a spectrum.

sections.h2: 6 · The surprise — this gap is the whole foundation of machine learning

blocks.html: Understanding train-versus-test loss — the gap between performance on data the model saw and data it did not — is the central concern of machine learning. It drives pretraining (why we train on oceans of text, to let the model discover generalizable patterns), scaling laws (bigger models generalize better), fine-tuning (tuning a model that already generalized, rather than starting from scratch), and the entire field of regularization (techniques like dropout and weight decay that deliberately constrain a model to prevent memorization and force it to find the general rule). The same gap appears in every domain: vision models on new images, recommender systems on new users, drug discovery on new molecules. When people say 'the model learned,' what they mean is 'it generalized' — the thing that makes the model useful for anything beyond the training set. Measure the gap, and you know whether you have learned anything at all.

sections.h2: 7 · Where it is used in practice — learning rules, not memorizing strings

blocks.html: A language model that has truly learned grammar and syntax should handle novel sentences it never saw during training. A vision model that has learned shape recognition should identify objects in new angles and lighting it never encountered. A recommendation system that learned user preferences should rank new items it has never seen before. A machine translation model should translate new word combinations even though the exact phrase never appeared in its training text.

To test whether a model learned or merely memorized, you measure how well it handles held-out data—information it never saw during training. You feed it two kinds of novel input: meaningful text that follows the rules it learned, and gibberish that has no structure. If the model learned the rules, the meaningful input should look natural (low loss) and the gibberish should look bewildering (high loss). A large gap between the two shows the model captured generalizable patterns, not just stored strings.
Models that memorize training data are useless the moment they encounter anything new; models that generalize keep working on the world outside their training set.

recipe.summary: Run the real pretrained GPT-2 (124M) on two held-out sentences it never saw in training: one grammatically correct and novel, one a random string of tokens. For each, measure the average loss (per-token surprise) across the entire sequence. A generalized model shows far higher loss on noise than on meaningful text.
recipe.eq:
loss_per_token = -log P(token | previous_tokens)
novel_grammatical_sentence: mean loss = 6.24
random_tokens: mean loss = 13.71
ratio = 13.71 / 6.24 = 2.19× higher on noise
recipe.note: Full script: scripts/experiments/stanford_gpt2.py (exp_generalization), the actual GPT-2 weights. Numbers are the run's output verbatim.
